docs.title: Quant Trading Knowledge Base
docs.text:
How quantitative trading firms trade US equities, with strategies and algorithms first.

Last updated: 2026-11

docs.title: What this is
docs.text: This knowledge base covers what quant firms actually trade, why each strategy makes money, and who is on the other side. It then covers the concrete algorithms inside the research-and-trading pipeline: signal construction, forecasting, validation, risk models and optimization, execution, and market-making logic. The goal is a medium-deep, accurate mental model: enough to discuss any strategy family with a quant, follow an idea from signal to P&L, read short Python for the core algorithms, and tell real insight from marketing.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: A finance professional who is comfortable with valuation, accounting, capital markets and filings, has CFA-level statistics, and reads Python without being a production engineer. Finance basics are skipped. Microstructure, stat-arb math, finance-specific machine-learning pitfalls, optimization, execution theory and market-making models are taught from first principles. Intuition comes first, numbers second, and math sits in collapsible blocks.

docs.title: The labs
docs.text: Twenty small Python labs on synthetic data make the core algorithms concrete. They range from a matching engine and Avellaneda-Stoikov quoting to purged cross-validation, mean-variance optimization and the Almgren-Chriss frontier. Each is a single deterministic script, small enough to run on a laptop, and its plots are embedded in the relevant pages. See Labs for the list, or browse the code on GitHub.

docs.title: How this was built and its limitations
docs.text:
• AI-assisted. The KB was researched and written with AI assistance from public sources: papers, regulators' documents, filings, firm talks and blogs, reputable press and practitioner books. The master bibliography lists them.
  • Public sources only. Firm details come from public sources. Nothing here is inside information, and no firm's proprietary strategy is described as fact unless it is publicly documented.
  • Synthetic labs. The labs run on simulated markets. They show mechanisms, not achievable returns.
  • Dated. Market structure and regulation change. Time-sensitive facts are dated "as of 2026-11" and will go stale.
  • Not investment advice. This is educational material. Errors are possible; corrections are welcome as GitHub issues.

docs.title: ETF, futures and options linkages
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • An ETF, its stock basket, the index future and index options are different wrappers on one exposure. Arbitrage keeps them within a few basis points of each other and passes flow from one to the next.
  • ETF ↔ basket: authorized participants create and redeem shares in kind. The no-arbitrage band is the cost of trading the basket plus creation fees.
  • Futures ↔ cash: fair value is spot times carry (financing minus dividends). The E-mini usually leads price discovery.
  • Options ↔ stock: put-call parity ties calls to puts, and dealers' delta hedging pushes options flow into the underlying. 0DTE reached a record 66.2% of SPX options volume in July 2026 [Verified]. Whether its hedging amplifies or dampens intraday moves is still contested.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: One exposure, four wrappers
docs.text:
The S&P 500 can be held as 500 stocks, as an ETF such as SPY, as an E-mini future (ES), or synthetically through SPX or SPY options. Each wrapper has its own venue, costs, hours and investors. All four pay off on the same index, so a gap between them wider than trading costs is a near-riskless trade, and the fastest, cheapest firms close it. A large buy in one wrapper is quickly felt in the other three.

flowchart LR

    BSK <-->|"cash-and-carry<br/>(basis = carry)"| FUT["Index future<br/>(ES)"]
    FUT <-->|"hedge substitute<br/>(futures usually lead)"| ETF
    OPT["Index and ETF options<br/>(SPX, SPY)"] -->|"dealer delta hedging"| FUT
    OPT -->|"dealer delta hedging"| ETF

docs.title: ETFs: creation, redemption and the arbitrage band
docs.text:
An authorized participant (AP) is a broker-dealer with a contract with the fund. To create, it delivers the fund's published basket plus a small cash component and receives a creation unit of new ETF shares. To redeem, it does the reverse. US equity ETFs mostly work in kind, which lets the fund shed low-basis shares without realizing capital gains. Cash creations, common for hard-to-trade assets, make the fund trade the securities itself and pass the cost back through a variable fee. SEC Rule 6c-11 (2019) allows custom baskets. It requires daily publication of holdings and disclosure of any premium or discount above 2% that lasts more than seven consecutive trading days [Verified].

NAV is struck once a day from closing prices. The intraday indicative value (iNAV) is a slow public estimate, and Rule 6c-11 itself does not require it [Verified]. Professional desks compute their own fair value in real time from the basket, futures and correlated ETFs (see fair value and microprice).

Worked example (illustrative). The basket is worth $100.00 per ETF share. One creation unit is 50,000 shares, or $5.0M. Trading the basket costs about 3 bp and the creation fee is $500, about 1 bp. Arbitrage therefore starts once the premium or discount exceeds about ±4 bp. Suppose the ETF bid is $100.06, a 6 bp premium. The AP sells 50,000 ETF shares for $5,003,000, buys the basket for $5,000,000, pays $1,500 in trading costs and $500 to create, and delivers. Profit is $1,000, or 2 bp. In practice an ETF market maker rarely creates per trade. It hedges with futures or the basket, nets inventory through the day and creates or redeems at the close.

sequenceDiagram
    participant AP as Authorized participant
    participant MKT as Stock market
    participant FUND as ETF issuer
    participant EXCH as ETF secondary market
    AP->>EXCH: Sell ETF shares at a premium
    AP->>MKT: Buy the creation basket
    AP->>FUND: Deliver basket plus cash component
    FUND->>AP: Issue a creation unit of new ETF shares
    AP->>EXCH: Deliver ETF shares to cover the sale

docs.title: Index futures: fair value and basis
docs.text:
The E-mini S&P 500 pays $50 times the index, expires quarterly and settles in cash. It trades nearly 23 hours a day on CME Globex [Verified]. Holding the basket costs financing and earns dividends, so the no-arbitrage futures price is

\[ F = S \, e^{(r - q)T}, \]

and the basis \(F - S\) is the net carry. With \(S\) = 6,000, financing \(r\) = 4.30%, dividend yield \(q\) = 1.30% and \(T\) = 0.25, fair value is 6,045.2 (illustrative). Suppose ES trades at 6,052. Desks restate that gap as the implied financing rate: about 4.75%, or 45 bp over the 4.30% financing rate [Estimate]. The futures are rich. An arbitrageur sells futures and buys the basket. Ten contracts capture 6.8 points × $50 × 10 = $3,400, before roughly \(600–\)1,200 of basket trading costs. The implied financing spread moves with demand for leveraged long exposure and with dealers' balance-sheet costs. That makes it a traded quantity in its own right, not a constant [Lore].

docs.title: Who leads: price discovery between futures and cash
docs.text:
Futures usually move first. One contract carries the whole index, needs low margin and has no short-sale restrictions. Hasbrouck (2003) found that the E-mini dominated price discovery for the S&P 500 [Reported]. At the millisecond scale, Budish, Cramton and Shim (2015) showed that the ES-SPY correlation breaks down. They also found that the median life of an ES-SPY arbitrage opportunity fell from 97 ms in 2005 to 7 ms in 2011 [Reported]. That race is what latency arbitrage competes in.

Leadership is not absolute. On stock-specific news, the stock leads and the index follows. In the closing auction, the cash market sets the print. Overnight, futures are the only liquid venue, so the cash open catches up to them. That last asymmetry would shrink if 23-hour exchange trading in stocks launches as planned on Dec 6, 2026 (see recent changes).

docs.title: Options: parity, delta hedging and the 0DTE debate
docs.text:
Put-call parity for European options (such as SPX) is

\[ C - P = S e^{-qT} - K e^{-rT}. \]

Violations are arbitraged through the stock or the future. In single stocks, a persistent violation usually means the shares are expensive to borrow. A synthetic short (long put, short call) becomes the cheaper way to be short, so puts trade rich. Option prices therefore reveal the borrow fee (see shorting, financing and settlement).

Delta hedging is the second channel. Market makers neutralize delta in the underlying or the future, and gamma makes that hedge trade along with the market. A dealer who is net short gamma buys as prices rise and sells as they fall, which amplifies moves. A dealer who is net long gamma does the opposite, which dampens them.

Here is a first-order illustrative example. With 3 hours left, an at-the-money SPX 0DTE option at 15% volatility has a gamma of about 0.0104 per index point. Take a dealer net short 2,000 contracts. After a 1% move of 60 points, it must trade about $750M of index exposure, roughly 2,500 ES contracts.

0DTE options were a record 66.2% of SPX volume in July 2026 [Verified]. Same-day index options averaged about 3.4M contracts a day in Q3 2026 [Reported]. The evidence on their effect cuts both ways:

View Evidence 0DTE amplifies volatility Brogaard, Han and Won estimate that a one-standard-deviation rise in 0DTE volume goes with about 14% higher daily S&P 500 volatility [Reported] 0DTE dampens or is neutral Dim, Eraker and Vilkov (2024) find that higher dealer open-interest gamma goes with lower intraday realized volatility, with no spillover to later periods [Reported]. Adams et al. argue that dealer hedging is mostly dampening [Reported]

The sign depends on net dealer positioning, which nobody observes directly. Neither view has won.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• ETF and index arbitrage and ETF market making are the creation band and the basis turned into businesses.
  • Lead-lag and cross-asset arbitrage and latency arbitrage trade the futures-lead structure.
  • Options market making, the volatility risk premium and vol arb, and dispersion and correlation trading depend on parity and hedging flows.
  • Flow-driven strategies trade around predictable ETF and index flows.
  • Algorithms:
    • Fair value and microprice builds the real-time basket value.
    • Hedging algorithms choose between futures, ETF and basket.
    • Options pricing and vol surfaces uses parity-implied forwards and borrow.
    • Order-book and trade-flow signals uses futures moves as a leading feature.

docs.title: Fees, rebates and ticks
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • Maker-taker exchanges pay the resting order up to about 0.29¢ a share and charge the taker up to the 0.30¢ cap. Inverted venues do the reverse. Fee-adjusted, the real price grid is finer than the penny.
  • In tick-constrained stocks, liquidity competes on queue position, not price. There the rebate can be a third or more of a market maker's gross margin.
  • The SEC's 2024 package (half-penny tick, 0.10¢ fee cap, round lots by price tier) is only partly live. Round lots took effect Nov 3, 2025. The tick and fee-cap changes are deferred to Nov 1, 2027 and under review (as of 2026-11).
  • Rule 612 bans sub-penny quotes at $1 and above, not sub-penny executions.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: Why exchanges pay you to trade
docs.text:
A maker posts a resting limit order. A taker removes it with a marketable order. Under maker-taker pricing, the exchange charges the taker an access fee, passes most of it to the maker as a rebate and keeps the rest. Inverted (taker-maker) venues charge the maker and pay the taker.

Model Maker Taker Published example (stocks ≥ $1) Maker-taker earns tiered rebate pays fee, capped at $0.0030 Nasdaq: top displayed-add rebates \(0.0029–\)0.00295; remove fee $0.0030 [Verified] Inverted pays fee earns small rebate Cboe BYX: add fee $0.0020 (tiers to $0.0013); remove rebate $0.0002 [Verified] Flat / most ATSs small fee or none small fee varies by venue

The economic price is the quoted price adjusted for the fee. Lifting a $50.00 offer costs $50.0030 all-in on a maker-taker venue. On an inverted venue it costs about $49.9998. A bid resting at $49.99 on the inverted venue really pays $49.992, which is 0.2¢ better than its quote without any sub-penny quoting. So takers sweep inverted venues first, and makers who pay to post there are buying a place at the front of the queue. A smart order router therefore ranks venues by fee-adjusted price and fill probability, not by the displayed price.

        X1 --> M1["Maker earns about 0.29 cents"]
    end
    subgraph INV["Inverted venue"]

docs.title: Ticks, tick-constrained stocks and queues
docs.text:
Rule 612, the sub-penny rule, bars displaying, ranking or accepting orders in increments finer than $0.01 for stocks priced at $1.00 or more. Below $1 the increment is $0.0001 [Verified]. Executions are not covered: midpoint pegs fill at half-pennies, and wholesalers give retail orders fractions of a cent of improvement (see venues and retail flow).

What matters is the tick size relative to price. One cent is 10 bp of a $10 stock and 0.2 bp of a $500 stock. A stock is tick-constrained when the spread market makers would quote if they could is narrower than one tick. These are usually low-priced, low-volatility, heavily traded names. In them:

  1. The spread stays pinned at one tick. Improving the price would cross the other side.
  2. Displayed depth piles up. With 400,000 shares at the bid and 25,000 shares a minute trading there, a newly joined order waits about 16 minutes (illustrative).
  3. Time priority becomes the asset. Orders at the front fill on ordinary flow. Orders at the back fill mainly when an informed trader clears the whole level, so they bear more adverse selection. That is why queue position has a measurable value.
flowchart TD
    A["Natural spread vs one tick"] -->|"narrower than 1 tick"| B["Tick-constrained<br/>spread pinned at 1 tick"]
    A -->|"several ticks wide"| C["Spread free to move"]
    B --> D["Long queues. Competition on<br/>time priority, fees and venue choice"]
    C --> E["Competition on price.<br/>Quotes step inside the spread"]
    D --> F["Key models: queue value,<br/>fee-adjusted routing, markouts"]
    E --> G["Key models: fair value,<br/>spread and skew setting"]

Round and odd lots. Only round lots count toward the protected NBBO. At 100 shares for every stock, a round lot of a $900 stock was $90,000, so better-priced odd-lot orders often sat invisibly inside the NBBO. Since Nov 3, 2025, the round lot depends on the stock's average closing price in the prior evaluation month, with reassignment twice a year [Verified]:

Average closing price Round lot up to $250.00 100 shares \(250.01–\)1,000.00 40 shares \(1,000.01–\)10,000.00 10 shares above $10,000 1 share

Since late April 2026 the SIPs have also disseminated the best odd-lot order. Odd-lot depth between that order and the NBBO is deferred to May 2028 [Verified]. Details are in NBBO and market data.

docs.title: The 2024 amendments (status as of 2026-11)
docs.text:
The SEC adopted the package on Sep 18, 2024 [Verified]. It had two parts that change unit economics:

  • Half-penny tick. Stocks priced at $1 or more with a time-weighted average quoted spread of $0.015 or less over an evaluation period would quote in $0.005 increments. All others keep $0.01 [Verified].
  • Access-fee cap. The cap falls from $0.0030 to $0.0010 per share for stocks priced at $1 or more [Verified]. Rebates are funded by take fees, so they must fall too.

Compliance was first due Nov 3, 2025. An Oct 31, 2025 order moved it to Nov 2, 2026. A June 2026 order moved it to Nov 1, 2027 and came alongside a staff review of both rules [Reported]. Treat both parts as unsettled. Recent changes tracks the dates.

docs.title: Worked example: a market maker's per-share P&L
docs.text:
Take a passive market maker quoting both sides of a tick-constrained $40 stock with a 1¢ spread. It earns top-tier rebates and exits 20% of its inventory aggressively. All figures are per share filled and illustrative.

P&L line (per share) Today: 1¢ tick, $0.0030 cap If the 2024 rules applied Half-spread captured +$0.0050 +$0.0025 Maker rebate +$0.0029 +$0.0008 [Estimate], the cap minus exchange margin Adverse selection (markout to mid) −$0.0045 −$0.0030 [Estimate], falls less than the spread Aggressive exits: 20% × (half-spread + take fee) −$0.0016 −$0.0007 Clearing and regulatory fees −$0.0002 −$0.0002 Net +$0.0016 −$0.0006

Read it as an income statement. The rebate is 37% of today's $0.0079 gross revenue, and without it the book loses $0.0013 a share. If the 2024 rules took effect, both the tick rent and the rebate would shrink. Survival would then depend on better markouts, which means better short-horizon prediction, or on more volume per quote [Estimate].

docs.title: Rebate capture: the logic and its limits
docs.text:
Rebate capture means routing and timing trades so you collect rebates instead of paying fees. Moving one share from taking (−0.30¢) to making (+0.29¢) is worth about 0.6¢. For a stat-arb book trading 5 million shares a day, that is about $30,000 a day, or $7.5M a year (illustrative). Three limits:

  • Selection and non-fills. Passive orders fill most often just before the price moves through them. Orders that never fill need a costlier catch-up trade later. Rebate capture only pays when the alpha horizon is long relative to the queue wait.
  • Tiers reward scale. Top rebates need a set share of consolidated volume each month, so large firms concentrate flow to hit the tier. A 2023 SEC proposal to curb volume tiers was withdrawn on Jun 12, 2025 [Reported].
  • Agency conflict. Brokers that route client limit orders to the venue with the highest rebate keep the rebate, and their clients get worse fills. Battalio, Corwin and Jennings (2016) documented this [Reported].

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Market making. Equity market making and ETF market making earn half-spread plus rebate minus markout. The table above is their P&L skeleton.
  • Fee-driven strategies. Fee- and microstructure-driven strategies trade on fee-adjusted prices and queue dynamics directly.
  • High-turnover books. For short-term reversal, the 0.6¢ make-or-take swing decides whether the strategy is profitable.
  • Algorithms. Fees and ticks are explicit inputs to:
    • queue position and order placement;
    • quoting and inventory control;
    • adverse selection and markouts;
    • smart order routing;
    • transaction cost and impact models.

docs.title: What each change means
docs.text:
The pricing grid: ticks, fees and lots. The round-lot change is live and it matters. In stocks priced above $250, the NBBO is now set by 40-, 10- or 1-share orders, so the protected quote is tighter and thinner. Signals built on NBBO size or on the spread shifted level on Nov 3, 2025, so treat that date as a break in any history. Half-penny ticks and the lower fee cap would rewrite market-maker unit economics (worked example in fees, rebates and ticks). Compliance moved from Nov 2025 to Nov 2026 by an Oct 31, 2025 order, then to Nov 1, 2027 by a June 2026 order. The Chairman has also asked staff to review both rules [Reported]. Treat the 2027 date as provisional.

Market data and disclosure. Since late April 2026, SIP subscribers can see the best odd-lot order, which narrows the information gap between SIP and direct feeds a little. The full odd-lot depth between that order and the NBBO waits until May 2028 [Verified]. The amended Rule 605 applies from Aug 1, 2026. It brings in large brokers and single-dealer platforms, adds millisecond time-to-execution, and measures price improvement against the best displayed price including odd lots [Verified]. That gives better public data for judging wholesaler execution quality and for TCA.

Routing rules. On Jun 11, 2026 the SEC proposed rescinding Rule 611 (trade-through) and Rule 610(e) (locked and crossed markets) [Verified]. One sell-side analyst expects a final rule in early 2027 [Reported]. If adopted, routers would no longer be forced to honor the best protected quote at every venue, and the case for fee-, fill- and markout-weighted routing would get stronger. The Gensler-era retail auction (Order Competition Rule) and the Reg Best Execution proposal were withdrawn on Jun 12, 2025 [Reported], so the wholesaler model described in venues and retail flow stands.

Trading hours. The SEC approved Nasdaq's 23-hour weekday schedule on Apr 10, 2026. Other exchanges followed, and the SIP plans approved matching hours [Reported]. The target is Dec 6, 2026. The schedule runs from 9 p.m. ET Sunday to 8 p.m. ET Friday, with a one-hour pause each weekday evening, and opens with static 20% overnight price bands [Reported]. 24X National Exchange has traded 4 a.m.–8 p.m. ET since October 2025 [Reported]. An Aug 7, 2026 SEC order lets 24X run overnight without SIP coverage from Jan 24, 2027, but only if the SIPs miss their date [Verified]. For strategies, overnight cash trading would weaken futures' monopoly on overnight price discovery. It would create new ETF market-making and event-driven windows, and risk systems would have to treat the "close" differently. Expect thin liquidity early on.

Options. 0DTE share keeps rising: a 66.2% record in July 2026 [Verified], and about 3.4M contracts a day in Q3 2026 [Reported]. Intraday hedging flow and the volatility debate are covered in ETF, futures and options linkages.

Settlement and shorting. T+1 is settled practice. After the Fifth Circuit's August 2025 remand, the SEC pushed the short-sale and securities-lending transparency rules to 2028–2029 [Reported]. Short-side crowding data therefore still comes from vendors and FINRA short interest (see shorting, financing and settlement).

Watch list. The SEC's Sep 17, 2026 innovation exemption allows capped on-chain trading of tokenized US-listed stocks for five years [Reported]. On Nov 3, 2026, the CFTC Chairman said single-stock perpetual futures may trade on venues also registered with the SEC [Reported]. Neither affects mainstream strategies yet. Both could become new hedging or arbitrage legs. On the CAT, the 2023 funding model was vacated by the Eleventh Circuit in 2025, a revised funding order followed in March 2026, and an April 2026 concept release opened a wider review [Reported].

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• The pricing grid. Equity market making and fee- and microstructure-driven strategies need scenario P&L for the 2027 tick and fee change, and they must re-baseline features at the Nov 2025 round-lot break. Their tools are quoting and inventory control and queue position.
  • Market data. Order-book and trade-flow signals and fair value and microprice change their inputs with odd-lot data. Point-in-time data must record the rule-change dates.
  • Routing. Smart order routing, latency arbitrage and retail flow internalization depend on how Rule 611 and Rule 605 turn out.
  • Trading hours. 23-hour trading affects ETF market making, lead-lag arbitrage, earnings and event-driven trading and algorithmic risk controls.
  • Options. 0DTE growth reshapes options market making and the volatility risk premium, and it changes the inputs to hedging algorithms.

docs.title: Shorting, financing and settlement
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • A short sale needs three things. The broker needs a locate before the order (Reg SHO Rule 203). Someone has to lend the shares, at a floating fee. And you carry recall risk for as long as the position is open.
  • Borrow cost is skewed. Most large caps are general collateral at a fraction of a percent a year. A thin tail of hard-to-borrow names costs 5% to 50% or more, and that tail is often where the "alpha" in short signals sits.
  • Rule 201 forces passive shorting after a 10% drop. Rule 204 forces the close-out of failed deliveries. T+1 settlement (since May 28, 2024) shortens every step.
  • Prime-broker financing spreads plus borrow fees can take a quarter or more of a long-short book's gross alpha.
  • The new short-position (Form SHO) and securities-lending (Rule 10c-1a) transparency rules are deferred to 2028–2029 (as of 2026-11).

docs.title: The life of a short
docs.text:
To a portfolio manager a short is one order. To the plumbing it is a chain of obligations that runs from the trade until the shares are returned.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PM as Portfolio manager
    participant PB as Prime broker
    participant LND as Lender (agent lender or fund)
    participant MKT as Exchange and clearing
    PM->>PB: Locate request (or check easy-to-borrow list)
    PB-->>PM: Locate granted, indicative fee
    PM->>MKT: Sell short on trade date T
    PB->>LND: Borrow shares, post cash collateral
    PB->>MKT: Deliver shares at settlement (T+1)
    loop Every day the short is open
        LND-->>PB: Fee reprices with supply and demand
    end
    LND->>PB: Recall (lender sells or votes)
    PB-->>PM: Re-borrow elsewhere, or buy in

docs.title: Locates and borrow fees
docs.text:
The locate. Under Rule 203(b)(1), a broker-dealer may not accept or effect a short sale unless it has borrowed the shares, has arranged to borrow them, or has reasonable grounds to believe they can be borrowed for delivery when due. The locate has to be documented. Bona fide market makers are exempt [Verified]. That exemption is what lets an equity market maker sell to a buyer before it owns the stock. In practice, prime brokers publish a daily easy-to-borrow list, and every other name needs an explicit locate against limited supply [Lore].

The fee. Shares come from lenders such as index funds, pensions and insurers, usually through agent lenders. The borrower posts cash collateral, conventionally about 102% of the loan's value [Lore]. The lender pays interest back on that cash, called the rebate rate: the benchmark rate minus the borrow fee. When a name is scarce, the rebate goes negative, which means the borrower pays on top of giving up interest.

Bucket Typical fee (annualized) Where you find it General collateral (GC) about 0.25–0.50% [Lore] most large and mid caps Warm about 0.5–5% [Lore] small caps, crowded shorts Hard-to-borrow / special 5–50%+, occasionally triple digits [Lore] squeezes, recent IPOs, heavily shorted names

The academic evidence agrees on the shape. In D'Avolio's 2000–2001 data, about nine in ten stocks lent at under 1% a year, and a small set of "specials" carried most of the cost [Reported].

The fee is a floating rate on an open-ended loan. Lenders can recall at any time. The fee reprices daily, so a name that costs 1% today can cost 30% in a squeeze. Engelberg, Reed and Ringgenberg (2018) show that this short-selling risk deters arbitrage and goes with more mispricing [Reported]. Drechsler and Drechsler (2014) find that much of the return to well-known anomalies is concentrated in high-fee stocks [Reported]. In other words, the "alpha" on many short signals is partly a fee you would have to pay to collect it.

docs.title: Rule 201, Rule 204 and T+1
docs.text:
• Rule 201 (short-sale circuit breaker). When a stock falls 10% or more from the prior day's close, short sales for the rest of that day and all of the next day may only be priced above the current national best bid. A few narrow exemptions are marked "short exempt" [Verified]. In effect, a short seller can no longer hit the bid. The short leg of a mean-reversion trade after a crash has to rest passively, and it may not fill.
  • Rule 204 (close-out). A fail to deliver from a short sale must be closed out by the market open on the day after settlement, which is T+2 under T+1. Fails from long sales and from bona fide market making get until the third settlement day after settlement, T+4 [Verified]. A broker that misses the deadline is barred from further shorts in that stock until it pre-borrows. Traders call this the "penalty box".
  • T+1 settlement. US equities moved from T+2 to T+1 on May 28, 2024 [Verified]. Trades must also be affirmed on trade date. For short sellers this means less time to source a borrow, faster buy-ins after a recall, and a tighter calendar around corporate actions and ETF creations.

docs.title: Financing through a prime broker
docs.text:
A prime broker finances longs and lends shorts:

  • Long side. The debit balance is charged at a benchmark rate (SOFR, OBFR or Fed funds) plus a spread, about 30–75 bp for a large fund [Lore].
  • Short side. Short proceeds earn the benchmark minus a spread. That spread is effectively the GC fee. HTB fees come on top.
  • Leverage. Reg T sets a 50% initial margin and FINRA Rule 4210 a 25% long maintenance margin [Verified]. Hedge funds mostly use risk-based house or portfolio margin instead. Under it, equity market-neutral books typically run about 4–8x gross leverage [Lore].
  • Swaps. Total return swaps carry the same economics but sit on the dealer's balance sheet, so pricing moves with the dealer's capital costs.

docs.title: Worked example: borrow and financing drag
docs.text:
Take an illustrative dollar-neutral book with $250M of capital, $500M long and $500M short (4x gross). In a dollar-neutral book the benchmark interest roughly nets out. What is left are the spreads and fees.

Cost line Calculation Annual cost Long financing spread 0.40% × $500M $2.00M GC borrow on 90% of shorts 0.30% × $450M $1.35M HTB borrow on 10% of shorts 8% average × $50M $4.00M Total drag $7.35M = 2.9% of capital

If the gross alpha is 10% on capital ($25M), carrying the book eats about 29% of it. The 10% of shorts that are hard to borrow cost more than the whole GC book and the long financing combined. That is why production systems treat borrow cost as a per-name negative expected return, cap or exclude HTB names, and build recall risk into sizing. A backtest that ignores this overstates short-side returns exactly where the signal looks strongest.

    B1 --> B2["minus long financing spread<br/>$2.0M"]
    B2 --> B3["minus GC borrow<br/>$1.35M"]
    B3 --> N["Net before trading costs<br/>$17.65M"]

docs.title: Disclosure rules in limbo (as of 2026-11)
docs.text:
• Rule 13f-2 / Form SHO. Institutional managers above set thresholds ($10M, or a 2.5% monthly average of shares outstanding, for reporting issuers) would report gross short positions monthly [Reported]. The SEC would publish aggregates.
  • Rule 10c-1a. Lenders would report loan terms, including fees, to FINRA for publication.
  • Status. In August 2025 the Fifth Circuit remanded both rules to the SEC without vacating them. On Dec 3, 2025, the SEC deferred compliance to Jan 2, 2028 for Form SHO (first filings due Feb 14, 2028), and to Sep 28, 2028 for 10c-1a reporting, with public dissemination from Mar 29, 2029 [Reported].

Until then, borrow data comes from commercial securities-finance vendors and FINRA's twice-monthly short-interest reports.

docs.title: Why this matters for strategies & algorithms
docs.text:
• Short-heavy books. Factor-residual mean reversion, pairs trading, cross-sectional alpha and value, quality and low vol all carry the drag above. Their short legs are where borrow constraints bind.
  • Rule 201 and recalls. These bite short-term reversal and earnings and event-driven trades when they matter most.
  • Market makers. ETF and index arbitrage and options market making rely on the market-maker locate exception and price borrow into parity.
  • Algorithms.
    • Mean-variance optimization and transaction cost and impact models take borrow as a cost or constraint.
    • Position sizing and risk budgeting handles recall risk.
    • Backtest pitfalls covers the cost of ignoring borrow.
    • Live monitoring and P&L attribution reports financing as its own P&L line.

docs.title: Algorithms: overview
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • This module covers the concrete methods inside a quant firm's pipeline: 39 algorithm cards in seven sections (A–G), three overview pages and four end-to-end walkthroughs (H).
  • Start with There is no single algorithm, then use the algorithm map to find any card by its ID.
  • Every card has the same shape: a header table you can skim in 30 seconds, then intuition, pseudocode of 40 lines or fewer, a worked example, practitioner tweaks, failure modes and questions to ask.
  • Twenty runnable Python labs on synthetic data back the cards. The walkthroughs stitch the cards together using the labs' numbers.

Level: Core · Read time: ~6 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: What this module covers
docs.text:
Strategies explains what quant firms trade and why it pays. This module explains how they do it. Each card covers one method (a risk model, a VWAP algorithm, a quoting rule) in enough depth that you can follow a quant's description of it, read its pseudocode, and ask where it breaks. Cards link to the strategies that use them, and the strategy x algorithm matrix shows the full mapping.

docs.title: How to read an algorithm card
docs.text:
The line under the title gives three labels. Level is Core (on the main reading path) or Deep dive (optional). Pipeline stage is one of data, signal, forecast, validation, portfolio, execution, market making or live. Last verified is the month of the last fact check. Next comes the header table:

Field What it tells you Purpose (the question it answers) Why the method exists. If you remember one line, remember this one. Inputs → Outputs What it consumes and produces, which is how it plugs into its neighbours on the map. Used by strategies Dossiers that rely on it materially. The matrix is generated from these links. Latency / compute regime Nanoseconds, microseconds, milliseconds, seconds or overnight batch. This sets the kind of engineering it needs. Key parameters The knobs and their typical ranges, so you can tell a sensible setting from a strange one. Main failure modes How it breaks in production. Usually the best thing to talk about. Lab The runnable lab, or "—".

The body always runs in the same order. It starts with intuition and a diagram that highlights the card's place in the pipeline. Then come the algorithm itself (plain steps, then commented pseudocode matching the lab code), a worked example with numbers, and how practitioners tune the parameters. The "textbook vs practice" section sources or tags every claim. After that: how to tell whether the method is working, its failure modes, sample practitioner sentences with glosses, and questions to ask, ordered basic to sharp, with 🔒 marking proprietary territory. Math sits in a collapsed block at the end. Confidence tags ([Verified], [Reported], [Estimate], [Lore]) are explained on the home page.

docs.title: End-to-end walkthroughs
docs.text:
The capstones. Each follows one business through a full cycle with numbers taken from the labs:

  • A mid-frequency stat-arb book: universe → three alphas → IC-weighted combination → risk model → optimizer with costs → VWAP/IS execution → next-day attribution.
  • A day at an ETF market maker: fair value from basket and futures, quoting, inventory, creation/redemption, hedging, markouts, end-of-day P&L.
  • An options market maker: vol surface → theoretical values → quotes → delta/vega hedging → Greeks P&L attribution.
  • Executing a $500M buy order: schedule choice, child orders, venues, the close, and the TCA report.

docs.title: Algorithm map
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • All 39 algorithm cards on one diagram: five research-to-trading stages (data and signals → forecasting → validation → portfolio construction → execution), a parallel market-making/HFT lane, and live trading as the loop that feeds results back.
  • Every card has a stable ID (D1…L3). The ID's letter tells you the stage; the five canonical pipelines are different paths through the same map.
  • Latency regimes run from nanosecond risk gates to research jobs that take hours. A card's regime tells you what kind of engineering it needs.
  • The map is not a one-way conveyor. Three feedback loops matter: TCA recalibrates the cost model, live monitoring retires decaying alphas, and markouts retune quoting.

Level: Core · Read time: ~7 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: How to read the map
docs.text: Solid arrows show what feeds what on a normal trading day; dotted arrows show research gates and feedback. Validation cards (V) never touch live orders; they decide whether a forecast reaches production. The market-making lane (M) is a separate, much faster loop that shares venues, risk controls and monitoring with the main pipeline. M9 Algorithmic risk controls sits in that lane, but every live order in every pipeline passes a pre-trade risk check.

docs.title: The feedback loops
docs.text:
Solid arrows explain one day; dotted arrows explain why a pipeline gets better or worse over months.

  fills["Fills and child orders"] --> E6["E6 TCA"]

  pnl["Daily PnL"] --> L1["L1 Attribution"]
  L1 -->|"PnL by signal"| L2["L2 Decay tests"]
  L2 -->|"retire or down-weight"| F5["F5 Alpha combination"]

  1. Execution cost loop. TCA feeds realized market impact into the cost model. If impact runs above forecast, the optimizer trades less and schedules slow down. Without it, capacity estimates are guesses.
  2. Alpha lifecycle loop. Attribution splits P&L by signal; decay tests decide when live IC has fallen far enough below the backtest to cut a signal's weight, freeing risk budget for new research.
  3. Adverse-selection loop. Markouts expose adverse selection by venue and counterparty; quoting widens or skews and the fair-value model is refit.

docs.title: There is no single algorithm
docs.text:
TL;DR

  • "What is their algorithm?" has no one-line answer. A quant firm runs a pipeline: dozens of algorithms, each answering one narrow question. What is the fair price right now? What will this stock do relative to its peers? How much risk is this? How do I buy it without moving the price?
  • The horizon sets the pipeline's shape. A market maker's loop closes in microseconds; a factor fund's closes once a month. A different tempo means a different bottleneck and a different place where money is made or lost.
  • Five canonical pipelines cover most US equity quant trading: the HFT market-making loop, short-horizon stat arb, mid-frequency cross-sectional equity, the systematic factor manager, and agency execution.
  • The edge rarely lives in one clever model. It lives in the joints between stages (forecast and cost model, fair value and quoting) and in unglamorous plumbing: point-in-time data, risk controls, feedback from fills.
  • A better question than "what's your algorithm?" is "which stage of your pipeline is the binding constraint?"

Level: Core · Read time: ~16 min · Last verified: 2026-11

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
Ask a quant "what's your algorithm?" and you will get a polite non-answer. Secrecy is part of the reason, but mostly the question is malformed. A systematic trading business is a production line of many algorithms, owned by different people, each solving a narrow problem, chained so that one stage's output is the next stage's input. Clean data becomes features; features become forecasts; forecasts become target positions; targets become orders; orders become fills; fills become P&L, which is attributed back to the forecasts that caused it.

A semiconductor fab is the right analogy. Nobody asks a foundry for "its process". They ask about lithography, etch, deposition, metrology and yield, because the product comes out of hundreds of steps and yield is multiplicative. Trading pipelines behave the same way. A forecast with real predictive power can be destroyed by a stale risk model, an optimizer that over-trades, or an execution algo that leaks intent. If each of five stages keeps 85% of what the previous stage delivered, only 44% of the original alpha reaches the P&L (0.85⁵ ≈ 0.44; illustrative).

flowchart LR
  A["Data<br/>D1"] --> B["Signals<br/>D2 D3 D4"]
  B --> C["Forecasts<br/>F1 to F6"]
  C --> D["Portfolio<br/>P1 to P7"]
  D --> E["Orders and fills<br/>E1 to E6, M1 to M9"]
  E --> F["PnL and monitoring<br/>L1 L2 L3"]
  V["Validation<br/>V1 to V4"] -.->|"gates"| C
  F -.->|"feedback"| B

Every pipeline in this KB maps onto these stages, and each stage has its own section of algorithm cards (A to G). The algorithm map puts all 39 cards on one diagram. Businesses differ in tempo and in which stage dominates. Below are the five canonical pipelines for US equities. Each gets a diagram, annotated pseudocode, its latency and compute regime, what dominates its P&L, and the cards used at each stage. The pseudocode is deliberately simplified: one function name stands in for a whole subsystem, and every number in it is illustrative.

docs.title: 1. The HFT / electronic market-maker loop
docs.text:
An electronic market maker continuously posts bids and offers in thousands of symbols. It earns the spread from impatient traders while trying not to be run over by informed ones. Strategies that run this loop: equity market making, ETF market making and options market making. The card-level version of this section is M1 Anatomy of an HFT trading loop.

flowchart LR
  md["Exchange feeds"] --> bb["Book build"]
  bb --> fv["Fair value<br/>M2 M3"]
  fv --> qs["Quote and skew<br/>M4 M6"]
  qs --> rk["Pre-trade risk<br/>M9"]
  rk --> ord["Order to venue"]
  ord --> fil["Fill"]
  fil --> hdg["Hedge<br/>M7"]
  fil --> inv["Inventory update"]
  hdg --> inv
  inv -->|"skew next quote"| qs
  fil -.->|"markouts M5"| fv
Stage What happens Cards Market data → book build Decode each exchange's direct feed; rebuild every venue's book; merge into one view M1 Fair value Mid-price tilted by queue imbalance (microprice), plus order-flow and futures/ETF lead-lag signals M2, M3 Quote and skew Center quotes on a reservation price shifted against inventory; keep or give up queue position M4, M6, M8 for options Pre-trade risk Position, notional, price-collar and message-rate checks before anything leaves M9 Order → fill New / replace / cancel; fills arrive asynchronously E4 for venue choice Hedge Offset unwanted risk in a correlated instrument (futures, ETF, basket, underlying) M7 Inventory and review Update position; measure markouts to detect adverse selection M5, L1 
# Event loop of an electronic market maker for ONE symbol (real systems run thousands in parallel).
# Simplified: production code is C++ or FPGA logic, lock-free and allocation-free. Numbers illustrative.
def on_market_data(msg, s):                        # s = per-symbol state, held in memory
    book = s.book.apply(msg)                       # 1. book build: add / cancel / execute at a level
    fv = microprice(book)                          # 2. fair value: mid tilted toward the thin side (M2)
    fv += s.signals.predict_ticks(book, msg) * s.tick   # + order-flow and futures lead-lag (M3)
    q = s.inventory                                # signed shares
    r = fv - q * s.gamma * s.sigma**2 * s.horizon  # 3. reservation price: long -> shade quotes down (M4)
    half = max(s.min_half_spread, s.half_spread(book, s.toxicity))  # widen when flow is toxic (M5)
    bid = floor_to_tick(r - half, s.tick)
    ask = ceil_to_tick(r + half, s.tick)
    for side, px in (("buy", bid), ("sell", ask)):
        if s.live[side] is not None and s.live[side].px == px:
            continue                               # unchanged price: keep the order and its queue spot (M6)
        o = Order(side, px, size=s.clip_for(side, q))   # smaller size on the side that adds inventory
        if pre_trade_ok(o, s.limits):              # 4. position, notional, collar, rate checks (M9)
            s.gateway.replace(s.live[side], o)     # 5. order out; fills come back asynchronously

def on_fill(fill, s):
    s.inventory += fill.signed_qty                 # 6. inventory update
    s.markouts.track(fill, horizons_s=[0.1, 1, 10])     # adverse-selection monitor (M5)
    h = s.hedger.order_for(fill, s.inventory)      # 7. e.g. offset an ETF fill with futures (M7)
    if h is not None and pre_trade_ok(h, s.limits):
        s.gateway.send(h)

Latency and compute regime. This is the only pipeline where the speed of light and the chip matter. The loop runs in memory on colocated servers. The critical path from an incoming market-data packet to an outgoing order (tick-to-trade) takes microseconds in optimized software and nanoseconds in FPGA hardware. For scale, an FPGA reference design reached a minimum of 13.9 ns in a June 2024 STAC-T0 benchmark [Verified]. That benchmark was vendor-commissioned and measures network I/O only, with no strategy logic. Speed matters because of races. On London Stock Exchange message data, Aquilina, Budish and O'Neill find that the winner of the modal latency-arbitrage race beats the first loser by only 5–10 microseconds, and that about a fifth of FTSE 100 trading volume happens in such races [Verified]. Model fitting (fair-value weights, fill probabilities) happens offline. The live loop evaluates simple, precomputed models because there is no time budget for anything else.

What dominates P&L. Read a market maker's day as an income statement. Revenue is spread capture plus exchange rebates. Cost of goods sold is adverse selection: losses to counterparties who knew more. Below that come inventory gains and losses, then fees and technology. Menkveld's case study of one large HFT market maker in European stocks found gross profit of about €0.88 per trade: €1.55 of spread capture net of fees, less a €0.68 loss on positions [Reported] (working-paper figures). The business runs on the law of large numbers, with a tiny edge per trade and an enormous number of trades. Virtu's 2014 IPO filing reported one losing day in 1,238 [Reported]. Fair-value accuracy, meaning not getting picked off, matters more than cleverness in the quoting formula. The other big lever is cost per message and per fill.

docs.title: 2. Short-horizon stat arb (minutes to days)
docs.text:
A book of hundreds to a few thousand liquid names, usually market- and sector-neutral, rebalanced intraday on forecasts with horizons from about 30 minutes to a few days. Strategies: ML-driven short-horizon alpha, factor-residual mean reversion, short-term reversal and intraday patterns.

flowchart LR
  ft["Features<br/>D1 D2 D3"] --> ml["ML forecasts<br/>F1 F2 F3"]
  ml --> cb["Combination<br/>F5"]
  cb --> op["Optimizer with cost model<br/>P1 P3 P5 P6"]
  op --> ex["Execution<br/>E1 E4 M6"]
  ex --> pos["Positions and PnL<br/>L1"]
  pos -->|"current holdings"| op
  cv["Purged CV and overfitting tests<br/>V1 V4"] -.-> ml
  pos -.->|"realized costs"| op
Stage What happens Cards Features Residual returns, order-flow imbalance, volume surprises, time-of-day effects; identical code in backtest and live D1, D2, D3 ML forecast One model per horizon; regularized linear models and boosted trees are the workhorses F1, F2, F3 Validation Purged, embargoed cross-validation; deflate for the number of trials V1, V4 Combination Blend horizons and models into one expected return per name F5 Optimizer with cost model Trade only where expected alpha beats expected cost; trade partway toward target P1, P3, P5, P6 Execution Passive first, cross the spread when alpha is decaying fast E1, E4, M6 
# Intraday stat-arb rebalance, every 5 minutes over ~2,000 liquid US names (illustrative values)
def rebalance(now, w_now, models, risk, cost, nav):
    X = build_features(now)                     # D2: residual returns, imbalance, volume surprise,
                                                #     time of day; same code path as the backtest
    X = X.apply(winsorize, k=4).apply(zscore)   # D3: cross-sectional scaling, outliers clipped
    preds = {h: m.predict(X) for h, m in models.items()}   # F1/F2: one model per horizon (30m, 2h, 1d)
    alpha = sum(wt * preds[h] for h, wt in HORIZON_WEIGHTS.items())  # F5: weights fit out of sample (V1)
    alpha = neutralize(alpha, risk.exposures)   # strip market, sector and style tilts; units: bps

    # P3 + P5 + P6: maximize alpha'w - risk_aversion * risk(w) - cost(w - w_now)
    w_tgt = optimize(alpha_bps=alpha, risk=risk, w0=w_now,
                     cost=lambda dw: cost.half_spread(dw) + cost.impact(dw),  # square-root impact
                     risk_aversion=5.0, max_name=0.004, max_gross=4.0,
                     dollar_neutral=True)
    trades = (w_tgt - w_now) * nav              # dollars per name
    trades[trades.abs() < 5_000] = 0            # no-trade band: small trades cost more than they earn
    for sym, usd in trades.items():
        urgency = alpha_halflife(sym)           # fast-decaying alpha -> cross the spread sooner
        send_to_execution(sym, usd, urgency)    # E1/E4/M6: passive first, take liquidity if urgent
    return w_tgt

Latency and compute regime. Decisions come every few minutes to an hour, and features update continuously. The optimizer must solve a 1,000–3,000-name problem in seconds. Models retrain offline, nightly or weekly, on CPU or GPU clusters [Estimate] (reasoning: a forecast horizon of 30 minutes or more leaves seconds of slack per decision, not microseconds). Latency matters in the execution leg, because passive orders need decent queue position. It does not matter for the forecast.

What dominates P&L. A tug-of-war between gross alpha and trading costs. At these horizons a good forecast is worth a few basis points per trade, the same order of magnitude as the half-spread plus market impact. An illustrative case: a forecast of +6 bps over two hours on a large-cap with 150 bps daily volatility. The square-root law puts impact at about Y·σ·√(Q/V) [Verified] (Tóth et al.). With Y = 0.7 (illustrative), trading 0.1% of daily volume costs about 3.3 bps of impact; trading 1% costs about 10.5 bps. The same signal makes money in small size and loses money in large size. That is why the cost model and the trade-toward-target logic sit at the center of this pipeline. Turnover is high: an average holding period of one to two days means trading roughly 50–100% of the gross book every day [Estimate] (turnover ≈ 1 / holding period). Signals of this kind also decay. In Avellaneda and Lee's academic backtest, net of their cost assumption, the PCA-residual strategy earned a Sharpe of 1.44 over 1997–2007 in the working draft. The published version reports an average of only 0.9 for 2003–2007 [Verified].

docs.title: 3. Mid-frequency cross-sectional equity (days to weeks)
docs.text:
This is classic quant equity market-neutral. Dozens to hundreds of signals (value, quality, analyst revisions, sentiment, short-term reversal, alternative data) are combined into one forecast per stock. A risk model and an optimizer then turn those forecasts into a neutral book, rebalanced daily. Strategies: cross-sectional alpha and neutralization, fundamental quant signals, analyst revisions and sentiment and alternative data. The mid-frequency walkthrough runs this pipeline end to end with numbers.

flowchart TD
  d["Point-in-time data<br/>D1"] --> a["Alphas<br/>D2 F4"]
  a --> t["Transforms and evaluation<br/>D3 D4"]
  t --> c["Combination<br/>F5 F1"]
  c --> o["Optimizer<br/>P3 P4 P7"]
  rm["Risk model<br/>P1 P2"] --> o
  tc["Cost model<br/>P5"] --> o
  o --> tl["Trade list<br/>P6"]
  tl --> ex["Execution algos<br/>E2 E3 E5"]
  ex --> at["Attribution<br/>L1 E6"]
  at -.->|"retire or reweight"| c
  at -.->|"recalibrate"| tc
Stage What happens Cards Data As-of-date fundamentals, prices, estimates; delisted names kept D1 Alphas Raw signals from prices, fundamentals, text D2, F4 Transforms Winsorize, z-score, industry-neutralize; track information coefficient (IC) and decay D3, D4 Combination IC-weighted or regression blend, shrunk toward equal weights F5, F1 Risk model Factor exposures, factor covariance, specific risk P1, P2 Optimizer → trade list Max alpha minus risk minus cost, subject to neutrality and caps P3, P4, P5, P6, P7 Execution algos VWAP for most names, IS for urgent ones, part at the close E2, E3, E5 Attribution Split P&L into factor, specific, cost and unexplained L1, E6, L2 
# Nightly batch for a market-neutral US equity book (~3,000 names); trades go out tomorrow
def nightly_run(d, positions):
    data = load_point_in_time(d)                 # D1: values as known on date d; delisted names kept
    raw = {k: f(data) for k, f in ALPHAS.items()}     # D2/F4: value, quality, revisions, reversal, text
    sig = {k: neutralize(zscore(winsorize(v, 3.0)), data.industry)   # D3: comparable, industry-neutral
           for k, v in raw.items()}
    ic = {k: rolling_ic(sig[k], data.fwd_ret, window=252) for k in sig}   # D4: live track record
    z = combine(sig, weights=ic_weights(ic, shrink=0.5))   # F5: IC-weighted, shrunk toward equal weight
    alpha = IC_COMBINED * data.resid_vol * z     # Grinold's rule: forecast = IC x volatility x score

    B, F, D = risk_model(data)                   # P1/P2: exposures, factor covariance, specific variance
    w = optimize(alpha, B, F, D, w0=positions,
                 risk_aversion=10.0,
                 tcost=impact_model(data.adv, data.vol),            # P5
                 constraints=[beta_neutral(), industry_net(0.01),   # P3/P7: neutral and capped
                              name_cap(0.01), gross_leverage(4.0)])
    trades = shares(w - positions, data.close)
    trades = trades[trades.abs() >= 100]         # drop trades too small to be worth a ticket
    algos = assign_algos(trades, default="VWAP",              # E2: most of the list
                         urgent="IS", close_frac=0.25)        # E3 for fast alpha, E5 for the close
    return trades, algos

def morning_attribution(d):                      # L1/E6: where did yesterday's P&L come from?
    return decompose_pnl(d, parts=["factor", "specific", "trading_cost", "unexplained"])

Latency and compute regime. Overnight batch. Data land after the close, the pipeline runs in a few hours, and trading happens the next day through VWAP and IS schedules or the closing auction. The heavy compute is in research: thousands of backtests over decades of point-in-time data. Production is light. The optimizer for about 3,000 names with a factor risk model solves in seconds [Estimate]. Reasoning: it is a convex quadratic program with about 3,000 variables, and the covariance is factor-structured rather than a dense 3,000 × 3,000 matrix. MSCI's Barra USE4 model, for example, uses 60 industry factors, 12 style factors and one country factor [Verified].

What dominates P&L. Breadth of many weak signals. The fundamental law of active management (Grinold and Kahn) says the information ratio is roughly IC × √breadth. Take an IC of 0.02 on 2,000 names re-forecast monthly (illustrative). Breadth is 24,000, and the theoretical IR is 0.02 × 155 ≈ 3.1. Three things then cut it down. Bets are correlated. Constraints dilute the signal: the transfer coefficient is often 0.3–0.7 [Estimate]. Costs take a further share. A realized net IR of 1–2 is considered strong [Lore]. In accounting terms, P&L = unintended factor exposure (should be near zero) + stock-specific alpha − trading costs − financing. The risk model's job is to shrink the first term.

docs.title: 4. Systematic factor manager (monthly)
docs.text:
Long-only or long/short portfolios tilted toward documented factors (value, momentum, quality, low volatility), often managed against a benchmark. There are few signals, they are transparent, and capacity is large. Strategies: factor investing fundamentals, momentum, value, quality and low volatility and factor timing and crowding.

flowchart LR
  fs["Factor scores<br/>value, momentum, quality, low vol"] --> pc["Constrained construction<br/>P1 P3 P4 P7"]
  bm["Benchmark and constraints"] --> pc
  pc --> rb["Monthly rebalance<br/>P5 P6"]
  rb --> ex["VWAP or closing auction<br/>E2 E5"]
  ex --> mon["Monitoring<br/>L1 F6"]
  mon -.->|"next month"| fs
  bt["Backtests and overfitting tests<br/>V2 V3 V4"] -.-> fs
Stage What happens Cards Factor scores Point-in-time composites per factor, winsorized and z-scored D1, D3 Research gate Long backtests, multiple-testing discipline V2, V3, V4 Constrained construction Maximize factor exposure within a tracking error budget and position limits P1, P3, P4, P7 Rebalance Turnover caps and no-trade bands; simple cost model P5, P6 Execution and monitoring Multi-day VWAP or the close; regime and exposure monitoring E2, E5, L1, F6 
# Monthly rebalance of a long-only multi-factor fund vs a large-cap benchmark (illustrative values)
def monthly_rebalance(d, holdings, bench):
    univ = universe(d, min_mcap=2e9, min_adv_usd=20e6)          # D1: point-in-time, liquid names only
    s = pd.DataFrame({
        "value":    zscore(book_to_price(univ) + earnings_yield(univ)),
        "momentum": zscore(total_return(univ, months=12, skip=1)),   # 12-1 month momentum
        "quality":  zscore(gross_profitability(univ) - accruals(univ)),
        "low_vol":  zscore(-volatility(univ, days=252)),
    }).clip(-3, 3)                                              # D3: winsorized composites
    score = s.mean(axis=1)                                      # equal weights: hard to overfit
    w = optimize_vs_benchmark(                                  # P3/P4: most exposure per unit of risk
        score, bench=bench, w0=holdings,
        tracking_error=0.03,                                    # ~3% active risk budget
        max_active_name=0.015, max_active_sector=0.03,
        turnover_cap=0.20,                                      # P6: one-way monthly turnover limit
        tcost=linear_cost(bps=8))                               # P5: a simple cost model suffices here
    trades = w - holdings
    trades[trades.abs() < 0.0005] = 0                           # no-trade band: skip < 5 bp changes
    return schedule(trades, algo="VWAP", days=2, close_frac=0.3)    # E2/E5

Latency and compute regime. Rebalancing is monthly or quarterly, often with a no-trade band so that many names go untouched. Production compute is trivial; a single workstation could run it [Estimate]. Academic reference portfolios show the cadence: Fama–French size and value portfolios are re-formed once a year at the end of June, and momentum monthly [Verified]. The engineering effort goes into data history and into trading large rebalances cheaply.

What dominates P&L. The factor premia themselves, which arrive in lumps over years, minus implementation drag: turnover, costs and the dilution forced by tracking-error limits. Multi-year drawdowns come with the territory. Value suffered a deep drawdown in the late 2010s that ended only in late 2020, visible in the HML series of the French Data Library [Reported]; see the failure gallery. Research discipline is the real edge. Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue that so many factors have been tested that a new one should clear a t-statistic of about 3.0, not the usual 2.0 [Verified].

docs.title: 5. Agency execution
docs.text:
A broker's algorithms execute a client's parent order by slicing it into many child orders over time and across venues. Every institutional investor uses this pipeline, and it forms the execution leg of the other four. The institutional execution walkthrough follows a $500M order through it. Related strategy: auctions and closing liquidity.

flowchart LR
  po["Parent order<br/>buy 2M shares"] --> pre["Pre-trade estimate<br/>P5"]
  pre --> sch["Schedule<br/>E2 VWAP or POV, E3 IS"]
  sch --> ch["Child orders<br/>M6 E5"]
  ch --> sor["Smart order router<br/>E4"]
  sor --> lit["Lit exchanges"]
  sor --> drk["Dark pools"]
  sor --> auc["Open or close auction"]
  lit --> tca["TCA<br/>E6"]
  drk --> tca
  auc --> tca
  tca -.->|"recalibrate impact"| pre
Stage What happens Cards Parent order and pre-trade estimate Expected cost and risk for the size, given volume and volatility P5, E1 Schedule Implementation shortfall (front-loaded), VWAP (volume curve) or POV (fixed participation) E2, E3 Child orders Size, price and post-vs-take for each slice; auction and dark tactics M6, E5 Smart order routing Pick venues and order types using fees, fill odds and toxicity E4 TCA Compare fills with arrival, interval VWAP and close; feed the cost model E6 
# Agency execution of one parent order, e.g. BUY 2,000,000 shares by today's close (illustrative)
def execute_parent(order, mkt, cost_model):
    est = cost_model.pretrade(order.qty, adv=mkt.adv, vol=mkt.vol)   # P5: expected impact and risk
    if order.algo == "IS":                                  # E3: Almgren-Chriss, front-loaded
        target = ac_schedule(order.qty, horizon=order.horizon, eta=est.eta,
                             sigma=mkt.vol, risk_aversion=order.urgency)
    elif order.algo == "VWAP":                              # E2: follow the expected volume curve
        target = lambda t: order.qty * mkt.volume_profile.cum(t)
    filled = 0
    for t in mkt.clock(step_seconds=15):
        if order.algo == "POV":                             # E2: fixed share of printed volume
            want = order.rate * mkt.volume_since(order.start)   # e.g. rate = 0.10
        else:
            want = target(t)
        need = min(want, order.qty) - filled
        if need <= 0:
            continue
        if order.limit is not None and mkt.ask(t) > order.limit:
            continue                                        # price guard: never chase blindly
        child = make_child(need, passive_frac=0.6,          # M6: post most, take the rest
                           max_show=mkt.median_trade_size)  # small, unremarkable slices
        for venue, qty, px in smart_route(child, mkt.books(t), fees=mkt.fees):  # E4/E5: lit, dark
            filled += send(venue, qty, px)
    return tca(order, filled, benchmarks=["arrival", "interval_vwap", "close"])  # E6

Latency and compute regime. Mixed. The schedule is computed when the order arrives and re-optimized every few seconds to minutes. The smart order router decides in microseconds to milliseconds. TCA runs after the trade, usually overnight [Estimate].

What dominates P&L. For the client, P&L is cost. Implementation shortfall, in Perold's 1988 definition, is the gap between a paper portfolio traded instantly at the decision price and the real one. It breaks into spread, impact, timing drift and the opportunity cost of shares never filled. Almgren and Chriss framed scheduling as a trade-off: trade slowly to cut impact, or fast to cut exposure to price moves. The result is an efficient frontier of schedules [Verified]. For the broker, revenue is commission, and algo desks compete on TCA league tables. The edge is less impact and less information leakage than rival algos. The cautionary tale is 6 May 2010. A large seller used an algorithm set to 9% of the previous minute's volume, without regard to price or time, to sell 75,000 E-mini futures contracts (about $4.1B). As volume exploded during the crash, the algorithm sold faster [Verified]. In equities, the same failure is a POV order with no limit price.

docs.title: The five pipelines side by side
docs.text:
Pipeline Horizon Decision frequency Where the edge is Hardest engineering problem Typical failure HFT / market-making loop Seconds to minutes of inventory; near flat by the close Every market-data event; microsecond reaction Fair-value accuracy, speed, queue position, cost per message Deterministic low latency across thousands of symbols, with risk checks inline Picked off on stale quotes; runaway order logic (Knight 2012) Short-horizon stat arb 30 minutes to a few days Every few minutes to hourly Many weak, short-lived signals netted against precise cost estimates Identical features in research and production; an accurate cost model Costs overtake decaying alpha; crowded unwinds (August 2007) Mid-frequency cross-sectional Days to weeks Daily, overnight batch Breadth: many signals combined, plus a good risk model and optimizer Point-in-time data and research tooling that resists overfitting Factor crowding, look-ahead bias, unmodeled risk such as short squeezes Systematic factor Months to years Monthly or quarterly Cheap, disciplined harvesting of documented premia at large capacity Trading large rebalances cheaply; turnover control Multi-year factor drawdowns ("quant winter"); crowding Agency execution Minutes to days per order Seconds for the schedule; µs–ms for routing Lower impact and less leakage than rival algos Impact and fill-probability models; venue analysis Price-insensitive schedules in thin markets (May 2010); leakage

Horizons and decision frequencies are typical orders of magnitude, not firm-specific facts [Estimate]. Two failures in the table are documented by regulators. On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital's router generated more than 4 million executions in 154 stocks within 45 minutes, and the firm lost over $460 million [Verified]. Khandani and Lo trace the August 2007 quant losses to rapid unwinding of similar long/short equity portfolios [Verified].

The five pipelines share a spine. Each has a forecast: even an agency algo forecasts volume and short-term price moves. Each has a cost model, a risk limit and a feedback loop from fills back to research. Each also fails in the same quiet way when the research version of a stage drifts from the live version. Since 2011, US broker-dealers with market access must run automated pre-trade risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5 [Verified]. That is why a risk gate appears in every live pipeline, not only the fast one.

docs.title: Questions you could ask a quant about this
docs.text:
1. Basic: "Which stage of your pipeline takes most of your research time?" The answer tells you where they believe their edge is.
  2. Basic: "What's the horizon of your main forecasts, and how often do you rebalance?" This places them among the five pipelines in one sentence.
  3. Informed: "How do you guarantee that features in the backtest are computed exactly as in production?" Research-to-live drift is the most common silent killer.
  4. Informed: "Is your cost model calibrated on your own fills, and how often is it refit?" This tests whether the TCA → cost model feedback loop actually exists.
  5. Informed: "When the optimizer refuses to trade a strong signal, how do you tell whether the risk model or the cost model is responsible?" This shows whether they debug at the joints between stages.
  6. Sharp: "What fraction of gross alpha survives to net P&L, and which stage leaks the most?" 🔒
  7. Sharp: "What's your transfer coefficient after constraints?" 🔒
  8. Sharp, market making: "How do one-second markouts differ by venue and counterparty type, and what does the quoting logic do when they deteriorate?" 🔒
  9. Sharp: "What test retires a signal, and how many did you retire last year?" 🔒
